blocks.text: Computed tomography (CT scan) combines X-ray technology with computer processing to produce high-resolution cross-sectional and 3D images of internal structures. It is especially useful for diagnosing diseases, detecting internal injuries and guiding treatment. An ordinary X-ray gives a flat (2D) image in which bones and organs overlap; in a chest X-ray (Fig 20.7) it is hard to tell the front and back ribs apart because they appear on top of each other.

A CT scanner takes many X-ray images of the same section of the body from different angles: the X-ray tube rotates around the patient while the detectors stay in place, collecting information from all sides (Fig 20.8). A computer combines these images into a detailed cross-sectional (slice) image. The scanner then moves slightly along the body and repeats the process for the next slice, and finally the computer combines all the slices into a 3D image of the internal structure. The name comes from 'computed' (a computer processes the data), 'tomography' (from the Greek tomos, a slice) and 'axial' (the scan is taken along the body's axis): computed axial tomography. Fig 20.9 shows a child having a CT scan, with the monitor displaying a cross-section of the head.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 20.8 labels the beam 'gamma ray' and shows gamma ray detectors activated on both sides. A CT scanner uses X-rays from an X-ray tube, with the detectors opposite the tube, as drawn above.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The CT scanner was invented by Sir Godfrey Hounsfield (England) and Allan Cormack (South Africa) in the early 1970s; both were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1979. CT scans create hundreds of slices in seconds, like peeling a digital apple layer by layer, and can detect strokes within minutes of onset, which is crucial for life-saving treatment.

CT scans offer important advantages over traditional X-rays. A single X-ray image is quick and still useful but gives only a flat, two-dimensional view; CT produces three-dimensional images that show the size, shape and exact location of organs, bones and other structures, making it easier to distinguish tissues even when their densities are similar. For example, a CT scan can clearly show the position and size of a tumour, which helps doctors target it accurately with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays. However, CT scans use X-rays, a form of ionising radiation, so they carry a small risk. On average, the radiation dose from a CT scan is about one-third of the natural background radiation a person receives in a year, or roughly equal to the radiation dose received during four long-distance flights. Doctors therefore take special precautions, especially when scanning pregnant women or patients with existing health concerns.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says a CT scan gives on average about one-third of a year's natural background radiation, or about four long-distance flights. Typical CT doses are much larger: about 2 mSv for the head (about 8 months of background radiation) to about 7-10 mSv for the chest or abdomen (about 2-3 years, with background at about 2.4-3 mSv per year). A long-haul flight gives only about 0.03-0.1 mSv, so the book's two comparisons also disagree with each other.
